title: Cumulative locality governs collective quantum charging
authors: Sebastián V. Romero, Xi Chen, Yue Ban
abstract: Quantum batteries can outperform their classical counterparts through collective quantum effects, yet the conditions enabling such advantage remain unclear. Using a generic class of free-fermionic chargers we prove that global operators are insufficient for scalable superextensive charging and that a cumulative hierarchy of many-body operators is required, with the structure of the battery determining the degree of advantage. This is obtained by relating the charging power to the norm of the commutator between the battery and charger Hamiltonians and deriving an upper bound only capturing noncommuting terms. Moreover, we revisit the concept of participation number and propose an effective definition that accounts for the relative strength of the contributing terms, correlating it with the charging power scaling. Not limited to quadratic Hamiltonians, our results establish cumulative locality as a key resource for quantum charging advantage.
summary: This paper establishes that achieving super-extensive charging power in quantum batteries requires a specific, hierarchical structure of interactions called 'cumulative locality.' The authors derive mathematical bounds on the charging power by analyzing the commutator of the system Hamiltonians, linking the scaling advantage directly to the participation ratio of the contributing many-body operators.
main_problem: The research aims to determine the precise conditions required for quantum batteries to achieve superextensive charging power, moving beyond the limitations of global operators.
main_result: Superextensive charging advantage requires a 'cumulative locality' structure in the charger Hamiltonian, and the scaling is quantitatively linked to the participation ratio of the relevant many-body operators.
method: The authors derive upper bounds on the charging power by analyzing the norm of the commutator between the battery and charger Hamiltonians, relating this bound to the system's locality structure.
model_or_system: The system models quantum batteries (QBs) using free-fermionic chargers and a local battery Hamiltonian ($H_b$). The analysis extends to general quadratic Hamiltonians and the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) model.
key_observables: Instantaneous charging power $P(t)$, the upper bound $\|[H_b, H_c]\|$, and the effective participation number ($\mathcal{N}_1$) or participation ratio ($\eta$).
important_parameters: The locality cutoff ($n_L$) and the power-law decay exponent ($p$) characterizing the coupling strength of the charger Hamiltonian.
main_assumptions: The analysis often relies on assuming specific decay rates for couplings (e.g., power-law decay $L^{-p}$) and sometimes assumes dominance by specific operator families ($C_2$).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate how the upper bound scales with $n_L$ (FIG. 2), how the participation ratio $\eta$ and the power-scaling exponent $\ell(n_L)$ change with $n_L$ (FIG. 3), and the asymptotic behavior of $\eta$ versus the decay exponent $p$ (FIG. S3, S4).
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the necessity of cumulative locality for scaling, deriving the commutator bound, and then quantitatively analyzing the scaling of this bound and the participation ratio ($\eta$) across different locality decay regimes ($p$), culminating in asymptotic results for $	ext{E}[\eta_N(p)]$.
why_interesting: This work provides a rigorous, quantitative framework for understanding how spatial correlations (locality) in interacting quantum systems dictate macroscopic performance metrics, which is highly relevant for designing quantum devices.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematic illustration of cumulative locality. A set of spins (spheres) interacts through families of many-body operators generated by the charging Hamiltonian. The diameter of Hanoi-tower plates represents the operator locality, while the stacked plates depict the cumulative hierarchy up to the maximum locality nL. a, For nL = 2, only local and two-body terms are present, leading to extensive scaling. b, For a fixed 2 < nL < N, the locality hierarchy is truncated, leading to a crossover around nL ∼N and asymptotically extensive scaling for nL ≪N. c, For nL = N, the system reaches the fully global regime (all operators in equation (2) are present), enabling superextensive scaling.

FIG. 2. Scaling of the charging power bound. a, The bound UnL(N) in equation (5) for nL = {2, 100, 1000}. Data points are fitted to f(N) = aN b, excluding N ≤100 for nL = 100 and N ≤10 otherwise. The nL = 100 and nL = 1000 curves overlap for N ≤100. The inset compares the bound with the exact commutator norm ∥[Hb, Hc]∥and the maximum charging power P∗for N ∈[2, 16]. b, Exact commutator norms (solid) and P∗(dashed) for the quadratic battery subclass, with nL = {2, 100, 1000}. All cases remain extensive despite the increasing locality cutoff. All results (both a and b) are averaged over 32 disorder realizations, with shaded areas indicating the max-min range.

FIG. 3. Link between participation ratio and charging power scaling. a, Participation ratio η as a function of N for locality cutoffs nL ranging from nL = 2 to 10000. b, Corresponding upper bounds UnL(N) for the same locality cutoffs. The inset shows the fitted scaling exponent ℓ(nL) obtained by fitting UnL(N) to aN 1+ℓusing data with N > nL, while for the fully global endpoint nL = N = 10000, all system sizes are included in the fit. All results are averaged over a hundred disorder realizations.

FIG. 4. Scaling under power-law locality-decaying couplings. Participation ratios ηN(p) (a-c) and charging power upper bounds eUp(N) (d-f) for N ∈[2, 10000] and p ∈[0, 4]. Zoomed insets in a and b magnify the large-N behavior with ηcrit shown as a dotted line in a. All results are averaged over a hundred disorder realizations.

FIG. 5. Performance of SYK and global chargers. Ex- act operator norms ∥[Hb, Hc]∥and maximum charging powers P∗(solid and dashed lines, respectively) are computed for a, the q = 4 SYK model using the batteries Hx b (blue) and Hz b (orange); and b, the global charger with σ2 = N/3 (blue) and σ2 = 1/3 (orange). While SYK results are averaged over 128 disorder realizations, global charger results are averaged over 5 · 105 due to the increasing variance with system size.
